agent-skills-skill-md.title: Agent Skills (SKILL.md)
agent-skills-skill-md.why: An open, portable format for giving agents procedural know-how: a folder with a SKILL.md (instructions + metadata) plus optional scripts and references, loaded on demand.
agent-skills-skill-md.explain:
## Explanation

**Intuition.** Tools give an agent *hands*; skills give it *know-how*. A skill is a folder whose `SKILL.md` starts with a short name + description. The agent only sees those one-line descriptions up front; when a task matches, it loads the full instructions (and any scripts/reference files) – **progressive disclosure**, so hundreds of skills cost almost no context.

**How it works.**
```
my-skill/
  SKILL.md        # YAML frontmatter (name, description) + markdown instructions
  scripts/        # optional code the agent can run
  references/     # optional docs loaded only when needed
```
The [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) is shared across tools, so the same skill works in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Hermes and others; Microsoft's Agent Framework [supports it too](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/agent-framework/agents/skills). MCP's 2026 extensions framework adds *Skills over MCP*, so servers can ship skills alongside tools.

**Why it matters.** It's the cheapest way to make an agent reliably good at *your* workflow: no fine-tuning, no new code – just well-written instructions that load when relevant. Your AI Brain itself is driven by a Hermes skill called `ai-brain`.

**Pitfalls.** Vague descriptions mean the skill never triggers; giant skills waste context – split into references; scripts in third-party skills run with the agent's permissions, so review before installing.

**Key ideas**
- Tools = hands, skills = know-how
- Progressive disclosure: descriptions first, body on demand
- Portable across agents via an open spec
- No training needed: instructions + scripts

## Learning steps

1. Read the Agent Skills overview and specification.
2. Open the ai-brain skill in Hermes (skills/research/ai-brain/SKILL.md) and see how it drives this app.
3. Hands-on: write a skill 'paper-summary' that makes your agent summarise an arXiv paper into a fixed template, then use it on the LoRA paper.

## Self-test

- What is progressive disclosure and why does it save tokens?
- When would you write a skill instead of an MCP server?
- What makes a skill description trigger reliably?

agentic-ai-state-of-the-field-nov-2026.title: Agentic AI: State of the Field (Nov 2026)
agentic-ai-state-of-the-field-nov-2026.why: Snapshot of where agentic AI stands in late 2026: protocols standardising (MCP, A2A, Skills), agents moving into production with governance as the bottleneck, and research agents running full experiment loops.
agentic-ai-state-of-the-field-nov-2026.explain:
## Explanation

**The big picture (late 2026).**

1. **Protocols are the new platform.** MCP (agent ↔ tools) went stateless and HTTP-native in its [2026-07-28 spec](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/); A2A (agent ↔ agent) now lives under the [Agentic AI Foundation](https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A); [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) standardised how agents learn procedures. Learning these three gives you the 'plumbing' of modern agents.
2. **From demos to production – governance is the bottleneck.** Industry reports through 2026 focus on guardrails, context engineering and oversight; e.g. a Nov 2026 GCC study reported 75% of firms running agents but only 10% scaling *governed* agentic AI ([Agentic News](https://agentic.ai/news)).
3. **Agent identity & security.** MCP's [roadmap](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/mcp-roadmap/) prioritises agents acting with their own identity on behalf of absent users (delegation, DPoP, workload identity) – the next big security topic.
4. **Research & science agents.** Autonomous research agents (e.g. YouRA vs Sakana's AI Scientist-V2) and lab-in-the-loop systems (RhoAgent designing RNA, reported in Nature Biotechnology) run hypothesis → experiment → revise loops; auditability of evidence is the open question.
5. **Local agentic models.** Small/quantised open models aimed at local coding and tool use keep appearing (e.g. ternary 'Bonsai 2.5 27B', Apache-2.0) – relevant to your Small Models track.

**How to use this node.** Treat it as a hub: each point links to a deeper node. Re-run *Scan frontier* weekly and ask Hermes to refresh this snapshot monthly.

**Key ideas**
- MCP + A2A + Skills = the agent stack
- Governance/oversight is the scaling bottleneck
- Agent identity is the next security frontier
- Research agents close the experiment loop
- Local agentic small models

## Learning steps

1. Read the MCP and Agent Skills nodes first.
2. Skim the MCP roadmap's five priority areas.
3. Hands-on: build a 2-tool agent and add one guardrail (human approval before any write action).

## Self-test

- What are the three protocols/standards shaping agents in 2026 and what does each connect?
- Why is governance, not capability, the bottleneck for production agents?
- What problem does agent identity solve?

model-context-protocol-mcp.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
model-context-protocol-mcp.why: Open standard for connecting agents to tools and data through servers.
model-context-protocol-mcp.explain:
## Explanation

**Intuition.** Before MCP, every agent app had to write its own integration for GitHub, Slack, a database, etc. (N apps × M tools). MCP is the 'USB-C port for AI': a tool author writes one **MCP server**, and every MCP-speaking **client** (Claude, Hermes, Cursor, VS Code, ChatGPT…) can use it. N + M instead of N × M.

**How it works.** Messages are JSON-RPC. A server exposes three kinds of things:
- **Tools** – functions the model may call (`tools/list`, `tools/call`), each with a JSON Schema for its arguments.
- **Resources** – data the client can read (files, rows, docs).
- **Prompts** – reusable templated workflows.

The agent loop is: client lists tools → puts their schemas into the model's context → the model emits a tool call → the client sends `tools/call` → the result goes back into the context.

**What changed in the [2026-07-28 specification](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/)** (the big one to know):
- **Stateless core** – the `initialize` handshake and `Mcp-Session-Id` are gone. Every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`, so any request can hit any server instance behind a load balancer. Need state? Return an explicit handle from a tool and let the model pass it back.
- **`server/discover`** – optional call to learn a server's capabilities up front.
- **Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR)** – instead of the server calling the client mid-request (elicitation, sampling), it returns `resultType: "input_required"`, and the client retries with `inputResponses`.
- **Header routing** – `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` HTTP headers so gateways and WAFs can route/authorize without parsing bodies.
- **Cacheable lists** – `ttlMs` + `cacheScope` and deterministic tool order, which also keeps LLM prompt caches stable.
- **Extensions framework** – opt-in features such as **Tasks** (long-running async work with `tasks/get` / `tasks/update`), **MCP Apps** (interactive UI inline in chat) and **Skills over MCP**.
- **Auth hardening** – RFC 9207 issuer validation; Dynamic Client Registration deprecated in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents.
- **Deprecated** (≥12-month window): Roots, Sampling, Logging, and the legacy HTTP+SSE transport.

**Where it's heading** ([Aug 2026 roadmap](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/mcp-roadmap/)): server-initiated events/webhooks, agent identity & delegation (DPoP, workload identity), one clear tool-result contract, and *progressive discovery* so a server with 100 tools doesn't flood the model's context.

**Pitfalls.** Tool descriptions are prompt text – vague ones cause wrong calls; too many tools degrade selection; tool outputs are untrusted input (prompt injection); older tutorials (2024–2025) show the stateful handshake that no longer exists.

**Key ideas**
- N+M integration instead of N×M
- Tools / Resources / Prompts
- 2026-07-28: stateless, no handshake, server/discover
- MRTR replaces server→client requests
- Extensions: Tasks, MCP Apps, Skills over MCP
- Tool descriptions are prompts; outputs are untrusted

## Learning steps

1. Read the MCP docs 'Introduction' and the architecture page.
2. Read the 2026-07-28 release blog post; note what 'stateless' means and what MRTR replaces.
3. Install an existing MCP server (e.g. filesystem or GitHub) into Hermes or Claude and watch the tool calls.
4. Hands-on: write a tiny MCP server with the official Python SDK exposing two tools over your AI Brain: search_brain(q) and get_node(id). Connect it to Hermes.

## Self-test

- Why does MCP reduce integration work from N×M to N+M?
- What did the 2026-07-28 spec remove, and how does a server keep state across calls now?
- Explain Multi Round-Trip Requests with an example of a tool that needs user confirmation.
- Why do deterministic tool ordering and cacheable lists matter for LLM cost?
- Name two security risks of connecting an agent to third-party MCP servers.

reasoning-models-grpo.explain:
## Background

Policy gradient methods are a class of reinforcement learning algorithms and a sub-class of policy optimization methods. Unlike value-based methods which learn a value function to derive a policy, policy optimization methods directly learn a policy function that selects actions without consulting a value function. For policy gradient to apply, the policy function is parameterized by a differentiable parameter.

_Source: [Wikipedia: Policy gradient method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Policy_gradient_method)_
